content.p: On 28 February 1944, during the German occupation of eastern Galicia, armed men surrounded the village of Huta Pieniacka. Polish prosecutors say they were Ukrainian policemen serving in the SS. The village was mostly Polish and held about a thousand people, along with refugees. By evening the buildings had been burned and the people in them were dead. Estimates of the toll run from about 500 to well over 800, and the argument over the figure has never been separate from a larger argument: who exactly was responsible, and what the killing says about the Ukrainian units that fought on the German side.

Polish prosecutors, and the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences' Institute of History as the historian Per Anders Rudling summarises it, both name the 4th SS Police Regiment, drawn from volunteers to the SS "Galizien" Division, as the killers. Rudling describes an emerging consensus among historians that units linked to the division took part, and the argument is mostly about scale. Some Ukrainian researchers, according to Kuryer Polski, deny that the perpetrators were Ukrainian.
content.h2: A glassworks village in the Brody district
content.p: According to a history of the village in Kuryer Polski, the settlement dates from the last decade of the nineteenth century, when Austrian documents record a glassworks there, the only one in the Pieniaki commune. Before the Second World War it was a large village on several wooded hills, with 172 farms and, in 1939, around 1,000 inhabitants. The same account says Poles, Ukrainians and Jews lived side by side and that relations were good until they began to sour after 1939, and especially from 1942.

By the start of 1944 the village had changed. Survivors and refugees from Volhynia and from neighbouring towns had come to it for shelter, according to Kuryer Polski. The inhabitants had formed a self-defence unit of about 40 people based on the local Home Army, commanded by Kazimierz Wojciechowski, whose codename was "Satyr". In early January a unit of Soviet partisans was quartered in the village, and it left on 22 February.

The Polish Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) and its Volhynia-massacre chronology describe Huta Pieniacka as part of a wider wave of violence against Poles. In the IPN's telling, units of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), led in Galicia by Roman Shukhevych, decided at the end of 1943 to drive Poles out of eastern Galicia, and Ukrainians distributed leaflets telling Poles to leave on pain of death. The IPN chronology dates the first UPA attacks on Poles in Galicia to 1943 and 1944, lists an intensification of attacks on Polish settlements in February 1944, and places the Huta Pieniacka killing on 28 February, attributing it to the 4th SS Police Regiment rather than the UPA. It puts the toll for eastern Galicia in April 1944 alone at about 8,000.

The Polish institute's own account of the final days says the village had been spared this violence so far but was not optimistic. A messenger from the Home Army's Złoczów inspectorate reached the village late on 27 February with a warning that units of the 14th SS "Galizien" Division were approaching. The order was that the local self-defence should not resist and should withdraw. A nearby settlement raided a few days earlier had been searched for weapons but otherwise left unharmed.

Rudling, writing in a scholarly journal, adds a different context. He says the village had become a refuge for Polish and Jewish survivors of surrounding villages and that it cooperated with pro-Soviet partisans. In his words, a Polish village that sheltered Jews and served as an outpost for Soviet partisans drew the attention of both the SS "Galizien" and the UPA. He quotes a Jewish survivor, Feiwel Auerbach, who said that 30 Jews had hidden in the forest near Huta Pieniacka and a neighbouring village from July 1943 to March 1944 and that Polish peasants shared their last food with them.

On 23 February a patrol from the 4th SS Police Regiment ran into the village's defenders. Kuryer Polski says two Ukrainian policemen were killed and eight injured. The IPN's account also says two were killed. Rudling says the sources agree that this first attack failed and two Ukrainian soldiers died, and that a second assault on 28 February left 8 to 12 Ukrainians wounded, one of them fatally. A Polish underground report quoted by Rudling gives a different count: four SS men killed on 23 February. The same report says the policemen entered the village in the evening in German uniform, spoke Ukrainian, began looting, and were taken for a disguised criminal gang, which set off the fighting.

A 2005 study by the Institute of History at the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences, as Rudling summarises it, tells the story from the other side. It says the Ukrainian SS men came to inspect the village after a denunciation from the population of Pidhirtsiv, who had told the Germans that the Poles were hiding Jews, backing Soviet partisans and storing weapons. The Poles, it says, took the looters for bandits in disguise and resisted.

The IPN describes what followed. On the morning of 28 February, at least 500 further men of the regiment closed in on the village, joined by a UPA unit and Ukrainian peasants from nearby settlements. Villagers were herded into the school and the church. Their houses were searched, looted and set on fire, and a few dozen people who had hidden and ran out of the flames were cut down with machine-gun fire.

The Kuryer Polski account gives more detail. It says the force of about 500 to 600 was led by a German officer and that the village was shelled before the attackers entered from four sides. People were questioned about Soviet partisans, and the commander of the self-defence was doused with flammable liquid and set on fire. Hidden wounded partisans and Jews were killed. In the afternoon the people gathered in the church and school were taken in groups of several dozen to wooden barns and other farm buildings, which were closed, shot at and set alight. Anyone who tried to escape was shot. According to the IPN, the policemen locked the residents in groups of 20 to 50, and the rest, more than 800 men, women and children, burned to death. Kuryer Polski says the burning ended at around five in the afternoon and that only the church and school were left standing.

An eyewitness account gives a similar picture. Zvi Weigler, whose account appeared in a 1957 bulletin and is quoted by Rudling, watched from about a kilometre away with a group of Jews in the forest. He recalled that German and Ukrainian SS men arrived at about six in the morning, fired machine guns and threw grenades, locked the farmers and their families in barns, and left only at night after the village had burned all day. Another account, a report from the Armia Krajowa underground to the exiled Polish government that Rudling also cites, says the 14th SS Division surrounded the village from three sides, and that children were killed in front of their parents. It dates the attack to 27 February, a day off from other sources. The same report says the only people who saved themselves were those who hid in the forests, pretended to be dead or hid in potato holes in basements.

There is no agreed figure. The Polish prosecutors in Kraków estimate about 850 killed, according to the IPN. Rudling reports that the same institute has also given a wider range of 700 to 1,500, counting about 1,000 residents plus refugees from nearby villages. The IPN's Volhynia website gives about 600 in its chronology. The Kuryer Polski history says the bodies of 868 victims were burned. Professor Grzegorz Motyka puts the toll between 600 and 800, and the inscription on the monument in the village names 1,000 Polish dead.

The Ukrainian commission, as Rudling reports it, counts nearly 500 killed and nearly 50 who saved themselves. A Polish underground report to the government in exile, dated 23 March 1944, spoke of about a hundred refugees murdered, though it calls the village "Huta Piemowska", which Rudling notes is a misprint, since no such village existed. Testimony from UPA men and survivors gathered by Soviet agents, which Rudling cites, speaks of more than 700 shot and burned and 120 houses destroyed, and one resident in the same file puts the dead at 600 to 700. One Ukrainian author, as Rudling notes, gives 700 to 1,200 Polish victims and cites a nationalist security-service document that dates the destruction to 24 February and calls the village "that center of Polish banditry".

According to Kuryer Polski, the Polish investigation's analysis of the evidence indicates that the perpetrators were soldiers of the 4th Galician SS Volunteer Regiment from the SS "Galizien" Division. Kuryer Polski adds that the prosecutors classed the events as war crimes and crimes against humanity and that 144 witnesses were interviewed, with research in Polish and German archives. Ukrainian and Polish government commissions both attribute the attack to the fourth regiment under Sturmbannführer Binz, according to Rudling, who adds that a 2003 IPN statement described soldiers of the division in white masking outfits surrounding the village, which was then shelled by artillery.

Rudling describes an emerging consensus among historians that units linked to the SS "Galizien" took part in the "pacification", with the disagreement mostly about scale. Rudling also reports remarks by Himmler, from a speech to the division's officers, which Rudling describes as a joke: that he would be quite popular if he gave the division free hands to exterminate the Poles. Rudling reads this, in light of Huta Pieniacka, as indicating that punishing crimes against that group would not have been a high priority.

Others dispute the Ukrainian identity of the perpetrators. According to Kuryer Polski, some Ukrainian researchers claim that the regiment's battalion only took over the village and that an unknown German police subunit then entered and pacified it. Others argue that the village burned in a battle between the SS Kampfgruppe "Beyersdorf" and the Polish defenders, that the civilian deaths were accidental, and that the burning was a penalty for helping Soviet partisans. The Kuryer Polski author says these writers ignore Polish, Jewish, Soviet and Ukrainian sources that confirm Ukrainian participation.

According to Kuryer Polski, the Soviet authorities put up a monument with a red star at the site that named German occupiers and Ukrainian nationalists as the perpetrators but left out that the dead were Polish. The star and plaque disappeared from the boulder in the 1990s after Ukraine became independent. Relatives raised a wooden cross in 1989, and in 2005 a monument with a cross and two stone tablets of names was put up through the Polish Council for the Protection of Struggle and Martyrdom Sites. The same account says the Ukrainian side held up the placing of the date of the crime on the monument for two years.

The same account states that the monument was blown up on the night of 8 to 9 January 2017, that one tablet was painted in Ukrainian colours and the other in the colours of the UPA, and that the letters "SS" were painted on it. The Kyiv Post reported on 10 January that Lviv police had opened a criminal case under Part 3 of Article 161 of the Ukrainian criminal code, which covers inciting national, racial or religious hatred. Kuryer Polski adds that the monument was rebuilt in February through the efforts of local authorities. The Kyiv Post's own wording was different on the cause of the village's destruction: it wrote that the residents died in punitive actions by German forces for cooperating with Soviet partisans.

In Poland, the Huta Pieniacka Association was formed in 2008 to keep the memory of the dead. Polish officials have since gathered at the site. In February 2020 the IPN's Krzysztof Szwagrzyk and other representatives joined relatives, witnesses and the association at the monument for an ecumenical prayer, and on 28 February 2025 an IPN delegation led by deputy president Karol Polejowski laid wreaths at the monument and lit candles among the few remaining tombstones. The Polish institute calls the killing one of the largest massacres of what it terms the Volhynian genocide, and Kuryer Polski says the Polish prosecutors' investigation, begun in 1994, was still being conducted by the Kraków branch when it wrote.
